narrative:
The model estimates you have a 22% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. First, having no past class failures actually worked in your favor and pushed the model toward thinking you would pass. Second, the fact that you are receiving extra educational support at school strongly pulled the prediction in the opposite direction, toward failing. This is unusual because very few students who ultimately pass (only 3.4%) receive this type of school support, so the model sees it as a warning sign that you may be struggling more than your record shows. Third, although you have a clear desire to pursue higher education, this factor also nudged the outcome slightly toward failure. Among students who passed, every single one expressed the same ambition, which means the model expects stronger academic signals from students who say they want to continue studying.

Taken together, the lack of previous failures helps your case, but the presence of school support and the gap between your ambitions and current performance outweigh that positive signal.

To improve, you should treat the remedial courses as an opportunity rather than a punishment. Focus on building consistent study habits beyond the current two-to-five hours per week, reduce your high weekend alcohol consumption, and talk openly with your teachers about why the support program was put in place. Small, steady changes in these areas can quickly shift your trajectory.
